Polishes Sectional Committee, CHD 023

FOREWORD This Indian Standard ( Second Revision ) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Polishes Sectional Committee had been approved by the Chemical Division Council This standard was originally published in 1976 with a view to facilitating trade and industry by establishing generally recognized usage and ehiminating ambiguity or confusion arising from various interpretations of definitions of the terms relating to polishes and its allied materials In the original standard some terms used in polishes and its allied industries were not covered These terms were covered in the first revision published in 1984 In this revision more terms have been added, which have come up in polish industry, during the last decade Some of the terms have been amended This standard prescribes definitions of terms in vogue in polish and other closely related industries excluding those relating to proprietary and patented items and those relating to other trades and industry Terms which may be commonly used in the polishes and allied industry but are selfexplanatory or imply commonly accepted diction try meanings have not been included To facilitate reference, the terms covered in this glossary have been arranged in alphabetical order

AMENDMENT NO. 1 JULY 1993 TO IS 8171 : 1992 GLOSSARY OF TERMS RELATING TO POLISHES AND RELATED MATERIALS

1 SCOPE This standard covers definitions of terms relating to footwear polishes and creams, polishes for application on floor, a u t o m o b i l e and aircralt, metals and glass, in addition to industrial polishing c o m p o u n d s . 2 TERMINOLOGY 2.1 Abrasive A substance used for the wearing away of surface by rubbing T h e common abrasives used in polish composition are emery, rough ( red oxide of iron ), chalk, dolomite, tripoli, pumice d i a t e maccous earth, emery, fullers earth and silica 2.2 Aerosol Liquid finely dispersed in compressed most gas ( propellant ) 2.3 Bloom An efflorescence which desclops on sole leathers or u p o n the bottoms, heels and edges of finished b o o t s and shoes and other type of footwears 2.4 Buffing The smoothening of a surface by means of flexible wheels to the surface of which fine abrasive particles are applied in liquid suspension paste or grease stick form This also applies to t h e rubbing off of surface after non abrasive paste or liquid polishes have been applied with a soft cloth 2 5 Caking The setting of pigment particles of a polish into a h a r d compact mass which is not easily redispersed by stirring The drying of a paste type polish into a hard unspreadable mass due to the evaporation of the solvent 2.6 Chilling The subjection of wax polishes to low temperatures in order to quickly transform them from molten state to semisolid state ( paste ) so as to impart certain desired characteristics 2.7 Cleaner A p r o d u c t , either liquid or paste, used for cleaning floor, shoes, automobiles, hard surfaces and porcelain articles In shoe care p r o d u c t s , cleaner also stands as renovation 2.8 Colour T h e aspect of t h e a p p e a r a n c e of objects which depends upon the spectral composition of t h e light reaching the retina of the eye and upon its temporal and spatial distribution 2.9 Consistency The apparent viscosity of a polish when shearing forces of varying degrees are applied to it in various ways, for instance, when it is stirred in t h e can, transferred from one vessel to a n o t h e r or brushed over a surface 2.10 Crazing Minute, interlacing cracks on the surface of a finish 2.11 Creaming The separation of a layer of the dispersed phase on an emulsion polish to t h e surface of t h e liquid continuous phase 2.12 Crystallization S p a r a t i o n of wax crystals leaving solvents to float 2.13 Diatomaceous Earth A natural silicious material composed of skelet o n s of small prehistoric aquatic p l a n t s related to Algae ( diatoms ) and found on some parts of the sea floor to-day It consists of about 88 percent it by mass of silicon ( SiO 2 ) It is usually colourless of cream in colour finely ground material is used in various polishes/cleaner's compositions as an abrasive 2.14 Drag Resistance on buffing alter application of polish 2.15 Dressing A composition applied on leather to preserve its softness and flexibility besides imparting freshness of a p p e a r a n c e 2.16 Drying Time Time taken by a polish to dry out sufficiently before buffing for shine 1

IS 8171 : 1992 2.17 Dubbin Waterproof grease used chiefly on army b o o t s shoes and on footwear for agricultural and shooting purposes 2.18 Emery Naturally occurring aluminium oxide containing some magnetic oxide of iron 2 19 Emulsifying Agents Substances of chemical nature used for effecting emulsification 2 20 Emulsion Emulsions are slable suspensions of tiny droplets of one liquid known as the dispersed phase, in a n o l h e r liquid known as t h e dispersion or continuous phase They arc of the following two types a) Oil-in-water, in which oil is the dispersed phase and the water is the continuous phase b) Water-in-oil in reversed which the phases arc 2.27 Mar Mutilation of polish recoating 2.28 Mop General term for a circular polishing made substantially of cloth 2.29 Mopping Synonymous with 'Buffing' 2.30 Oozing Same as sweating ( see 2.58 ) 2.31 Penetration It is a measure or firmness of paste polish a penetrometer 2 32 Pick Up Quantity of polish picked up when a polishing brush is gently dabbed or a piece of cloth is used for application purpose 2 33 Pigment The insoluble dispersed particles in a polish composition which give t h e dried film its characteristic properties of colour gloss and opacity 2 34 Pigmented Floor Polish These are highly pigmented floor polishes of the wax solvent paste type or emulsion type paste polishes with suitable colouring agents These are also known as tile polishes 2.35 Polish A composition generally applied it liequent intervals to produce desired, smooth, flossy surface on rubbing The common polishes are metal polish shoe polish and cream floor polish ear polish, aircraft polish, glass polish tile polish and industrial buffing compounds 2.36 Polish, Dressing These are prepared by wax ??? by suspension or dissolution of suitable ingredients in suitable vehicles Many of these can be sprayed on to the shoe uppers and often final polishing can be dispensed with 2.37 Polish, Dry Bright These are polishes which are also known by other names, such as no rub, rubless, salt-polishing, self-shine polishes On application with a brush or a pad, the coatings dry out to a smooth glossy surface without the usual rubbing or brushing 2.38 Powdering Partial or total disintegration of the polish resulting in a fine light-coloured material 2 film using wheel film repairable only by

Oil as stated above may be mixture of fats and waxes as well as oils and solvents and the emulsion forms when the same is in the liquid state. 2.21 Flash Point T h e lowest t e m p e r a t u r e at which the vapours emitted by a p r o d u c t ignite momentarily in the presence of a flame, when operating according to a specified test method 2.22 Fullers Earth A porous colloidal aluminium silicate ( clay J which has high natural adsorptive power Finely ground material is useful as mild abrasive for polishing smooth surfaces 2.23 Gloss The degree to which a polished surface possesses the properties of reflecting light in a mirror-like manner ( specular reflection ) 2.24 Heat Resistance T h e property of paste polish to resist warm ambience ( at specified temperature ) without changing its paste consistency 2.25 Levelling The property of a freshly spread aqueous polish to dry to a uniform and streak-free appearance 2.26 Lustre Brightness or shine of a surface

IS 8171 : 1992 2.39 Propellant A compressed/liquefied gas used for expelling the contents from an aerosol container 2.40 Rebuffability The ability of the polished surface to regain shine after its normal wear on buffing without the and of polish 2.41 Recoatability The application characteristics of a polish and appearance of the film after successive costings to a surface 2.42 Renovator A product which renovates an article to its original appearance 2.43 Room Temperaturc Ambient temperature of 21-38�C. It is also known as ordinary temperature. 2.44 Rub Out Stain A little quantity of coloured polish when rubbed over filter paper for noting its intensity of colour and shade characteristics 2.45 Shampoo A liquid product containing detergents used for removing dirt from shoes, car carpet etc 2.46 Sheen Surtace gloss examined. of paste polish when visually 2.52 Silicon These are semi-organic matenals which are employed in the manufacture of some special polishes 2.53 Soil Embediment or adhesion of solid foreign matter in or on the surface 2.54 Solvent The solvent should dissolve/disperse wax mass and remain uniformly distributed throughout the mixture A solvent is necessary to get the wax mass into a form that can be easily applied to the surface to be polished and to evaporate away and leave a thin film of wax on the surface 2.55 Souff Disfigurement of polish film resulting from the abrading of scraping action repairable without recoating 2.56 Spreading The action of flowing out over a surface during application 2.57 Stick Polishing A manual operation using small sticks coated with suitable abrasive, generally used in the polishing of jewellery. 2 58 Sweating ??? of solvent from the wax solvent or emulsion paste shoe polish in the container under specified conditions of test It is the same as 'Oozing'. 2.59 Tack Slight stickness of the surtace of a him of polish composition apparent when the film is pressed with the finger 2.60 Traffic Marking Marring or discoloration or both, of a floor surface by traffic 2.61 Vehicle The liquid portion of polish in which the solids are dispersed It is composed of solvent and other binding materials 2.62 Water Spotting Change in appearance of surface resulting solely from the action of cool water 2.63 Wax The term wax is now used very loosely to des cribe naturally occurring or synthetic material whatever its chemical composition, which

2.47 Shelf Life The time for which a polish will keep in good condition when stored in original sealed containers under normal storage conditions on the shelves of a shop of stock room 2.48 Shine It is brightness or radiance of a surface after being polished 2.49 Shiner Usually sponge of cloth, impregnated with polishing compound for producing shine on gentle application or rubbing. 2.50 Shrinkage Contraction of a polish, leaving edges of the container during its shelf life 2.51 Silica Occurs widely in nature as sand, quartz, flint, etc Finely ground material is used as an abrasive material for hard surface cleaner compositions

1992 2.66 Waxes, Mineral These are waxes of mineral origin ones used in polishes are paraffin linc and montan 2.67 Waxes, Synthetic These are chemical products developed to h a v e characteristics comparable to natural waxes for use in polish composition The c o m m o n s y n t h e tic waxes are t h e range of I G waxes and silicon waxes 2.68 Waxes, Vegetable These are waxes of vegetable origin and t h e common ones used in polishes are carnauba sugarcane, J a p a n , and candelilla waxes 2.69 Wear Attrition of polish film resulting use 2 70 Wetting The property of an aqueous polish to uniformly and completely contact t h e solid surface to which it is applied from normal The c o m m o n microcrystal-

appearance approximately resembles beeswax of ??? wax as limiting standards Chemically a true wax is regarded as an ester of fatty acids of high molecular mass with alcohols, of somewhat similar complexity Usually, also present are free high molecular fatty acids and the corresponding alcohols, and also solid hydrocarbons T h e natural waxes may be divided into three groups according to then origin namely, vegetable waxes mineral waxes and insect or animal waxes 2.64 Waxes, Animal These are waxes of insect and animal origin The common ones are beeswax, shellac wax vool wax and spermaceti wax 2 65 Waxes, Hard Hard' waxes in contrast to 'soft' waxes, take up more solvent but retain it more loosely, the cream made from them sets more quickly, is purer in body and, therefore, forms thinner films, dues and shines quickly, will not k e e p so long in the tins, and sets harder Examples are ??? wax bleached carnauba wax, and hard paraffin

Standard Mark The use of the Standard Mark is governed by the provisions of the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986 and the Rules and Regulations made thereunder. The Standard Mark on products covered by an Indian Standard conveys the assurance that they have been produced to comply with the requirements of that standard under a well defined system of inspection, testing and quality control which is devised and supervised by BIS and operated by the producer. Standard marked products are also continuously checked by BIS for conformity to that standard as a further safeguard. Details of conditions under which a licence for the use of the Standard Mark may be granted to manufacturers or producers may be obtained from the Bureau of Indian Standards.

Bureau of Indian Standards BIS is a statutory Institution established under the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986 to promote harmonious development of the activities of standardization, marking and quality certification of goods and attending to connected matters in the country
